title: Find north, south, east and west
subtitle: Use Polaris or the Southern Cross, the Sun and the Moon to get your bearings, and learn why sky maps look backwards

sections.heading: Polaris marks north, the Southern Cross marks south
body: Every direction in this app, "look southeast", "low in the west", assumes you know which way you are facing. After this lesson you will be able to work that out anywhere, with no compass.

At night in the northern hemisphere the surest guide is [[star:Polaris|Polaris]], the North Star. It sits less than 1° from the point in the sky that Earth's axis aims at, so while everything else wheels around during the night, Polaris stays put. Face it and you are facing north: east is on your right, west on your left, south behind you.

Polaris is not especially bright, only about the 50th brightest star, so do not hunt for it directly. Find the [[asterism:big-dipper|Big Dipper]] and use the two stars at the end of its bowl, [[star:Merak|Merak]] and [[star:Dubhe|Dubhe]], called the Pointers. Follow the line from Merak through Dubhe for about five times the gap between them. Polaris is the first fairly bright star you come to. Its height above the horizon always equals your latitude: from mid-northern latitudes, a bit less than halfway from the horizon to overhead.

In the southern hemisphere Polaris is below the horizon and there is no bright south pole star. Use the [[asterism:southern-cross|Southern Cross]] instead: extend its long bar from [[star:Gacrux|Gacrux]] through [[star:Acrux|Acrux]] about four and a half times its length (27°) to the south celestial pole, then drop straight down to the horizon. That point is due south; face it and east is on your left, west on your right.

steps.caption: An April evening, facing north. The Big Dipper is high and upside down. Find the two stars at the end of its bowl, farthest from the handle.
Extend the line from Merak through Dubhe about five times their separation and you arrive at Polaris. Drop straight down from Polaris to the horizon: that point is due north.

Now the night runs fast. The Dipper swings around like the hand of a clock running backwards, but the Pointers keep aiming at Polaris, and Polaris does not move. Drag the time slider to try other hours.

The southern way, from mid-southern latitudes on a May evening, facing south. Extend the Southern Cross's long bar from Gacrux through Acrux about four and a half times its length to the south celestial pole, then drop straight down: that point on the horizon is due south.

sections.tryIt: Tonight, find Polaris (or, in the southern hemisphere, the south celestial pole from the Southern Cross) from your street or roof and note what sits below it on the horizon: a chimney, a water tower, the end of the block. That landmark is now your permanent north (or south) marker for that spot.

figures.caption: The two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl always point to Polaris, however the Dipper is turned. Change the month and the time: the Dipper wheels right round, but Polaris stays fixed above the north point of your horizon, as high up as your latitude. (From the southern hemisphere the figure shows the Southern Cross pointing to the south celestial pole instead.)

image.alt: Long-exposure photo of the northern sky above a country road and trees: hundreds of stars have drawn concentric circular trails around one point.
image.kindNote: 37 exposures of 25 seconds each, combined, so about a quarter of an hour of sky motion

figures.caption: Leave a camera pointed north and every star draws an arc around one spot: the north celestial pole, where Earth's axis points. Polaris makes the tiny arc almost at the centre, which is why it seems to stand still all night while everything else circles it.

misconception.myth: Polaris, the North Star, is the brightest star in the sky.
misconception.fact: Polaris is only about the 50th brightest star, a medium-bright star that many people walk past. What makes it special is its position: it sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole, so it barely moves while every other star circles around it. Sirius, the brightest, is about 20 times brighter.

check.prompt: You find Polaris and face it. Which direction is behind you?
check.explanation: Polaris marks north, so south is directly behind you, east on your right and west on your left.

sections.heading: The Sun and Moon give east, south and west
body: By day, or when buildings hide the pole, use the Sun. It rises in the east, is highest when it crosses the north–south line, and sets in the west. But "east" is only exact around the March and September equinoxes. From mid-latitudes in either hemisphere the June Sun rises about 30° north of east, in the northeast, and the December Sun about 30° south of east, in the southeast. Sunsets shift the same way along the western horizon.

The most reliable moment is the middle of the day: when the Sun is at its highest, around noon, or around 1 p.m. during daylight saving time, it is due south from mid-northern latitudes, so shadows point due north; from mid-southern latitudes it is due north and shadows point due south. The Moon and the planets follow nearly the same track: up in the east, highest toward the equator side of the sky, down in the west.

steps.caption: Facing east at dawn. Three sunrise paths: the March equinox in the middle rises due east; the June solstice path starts far to the left (northeast); the December path starts far to the right (southeast).
From mid-northern latitudes, facing south at midday. Whatever the season, the Sun crosses due south at its highest point of the day: 72° up in June, 49° at the equinoxes, only 26° in December.
From mid-southern latitudes, facing north at midday: here the Sun crosses due north, 79° up in December, 56° at the equinoxes and only 33° in June. Shadows at midday point south.

figures.caption: The Sun rises exactly in the east only around the March and September equinoxes. Drag the date: north of the tropics, sunrise swings north of east from March to September and south of east from September to March, and the noon Sun is always due south, so its shadow points due north. The figure is computed for the location in your settings.

thinkAbout.question: The Sun is highest in the sky at about 1 p.m. on a summer afternoon, not at noon. How can that be, if 'noon' means the middle of the day?
thinkAbout.answer: Clock time is shared across a whole time zone and shifted an hour by daylight saving time, while the Sun's highest moment depends on your exact longitude. During daylight saving the Sun's peak lands near 1 p.m. on the clock, a little earlier or later depending on where you are in the zone.

check.prompt: From mid-northern latitudes, where does the Sun rise on a June morning?
choices: North of east, in the northeast
South of east, in the southeast
check.explanation: Near the June solstice the Sun is north of the celestial equator, so from mid-northern latitudes it rises well north of east and sets well north of west.

sections.heading: Why sky maps have east and west swapped
body: On a street map with north at the top, east is on the right. On a star chart with north at the top, east is on the left. Nobody made a mistake. A street map shows the ground as seen from above, looking down. A star chart shows the sky as seen from below, looking up, and turning over flips left and right.

To use a printed chart, hold it over your head with its north edge toward north; then every direction on it matches the real one. Starhop does this for you: whichever way the view faces, it shows the sky as you would really see it. Face south and east is on your left. Face north and east is on your right.

demo.title: Turn around and the sides swap

steps.caption: Facing north. East is to your right and west to your left, just as on a street map.

Turn around to face south. Now east is on your left and west on your right. This is how most northern star charts are drawn, because for northern observers most of the sky's action is in the south; southern charts are drawn facing north.

figures.caption: A street map is drawn for looking down; a star chart is drawn for looking up. Press Look up: north stays at the top, but turning your view over sends east from the right-hand side to the left. Hold a chart over your head with its north edge toward north and it matches the sky.

thinkAbout.question: You lie on your back with your feet toward the south and look straight up. Is east on your left or your right?
thinkAbout.answer: On your left. With your head to the north and your face to the sky, your left hand points east and your right hand points west, exactly as on a star chart with north at the top.

keyPoints: In the northern hemisphere the Big Dipper's Pointers, Merak and Dubhe, aim at Polaris; face Polaris and you face north. In the southern hemisphere the Southern Cross's long bar points to the south celestial pole.
Polaris stands as many degrees above the northern horizon as your latitude, and never moves noticeably.
The Sun rises due east only near the equinoxes: northeast in June, southeast in December.
The Sun, Moon and planets are highest when they cross the north–south line: due south from mid-northern latitudes, due north from mid-southern ones.
Star charts show the sky from below, so with north up, east is on the left.

questions.prompt: You are facing Polaris. Which direction is on your right-hand side?
questions.explanation: Facing Polaris means facing north, so east is to your right, west to your left and south behind you.

questions.prompt: Which two stars of the Big Dipper do you use to find Polaris?
choices: The two at the end of the handle
The two where the handle joins the bowl
The two at the end of the bowl farthest from the handle
The middle star of the handle and its faint companion
questions.explanation: Merak and Dubhe, the Pointers, form the outer side of the bowl. A line from Merak through Dubhe, extended about five times, reaches Polaris.

questions.prompt: It is late December at mid-northern latitudes and you watch the Sun come up. Where on the horizon does it appear?
questions.explanation: The Sun rises due east only near the equinoxes. In December it rises about 30° south of east; in June, about 30° north of east.

questions.prompt: A star chart is printed with north at the top. Why is east on its left side?
choices: It is a printing convention left over from telescopes that flip the image
The chart is drawn for the Southern Hemisphere
Stars move from left to right, so east must be on the left
The chart shows the sky as you look up at it, which mirrors a map made looking down
questions.explanation: A ground map is a view from above; a sky chart is a view from below. Hold the chart overhead with its north edge pointing north and the directions line up.

questions.prompt: At two in the morning the Big Dipper has swung to a completely different position than it had at nine. What about Polaris?
choices: It has set in the northwest
It has moved the same amount, staying beside the Dipper
It is in almost exactly the same place
questions.explanation: Polaris lies less than 1° from the point the sky turns around, so it barely moves. The Dipper circles it, with the Pointers always aimed at it.

questions.prompt: No stars are out yet, but the Sun is at its highest for the day. Which way do shadows point from mid-northern latitudes?
questions.explanation: At its highest the Sun is due south, so shadows fall due north.
